acceleration vector: The time derivative of velocity, a = dv/dt, describing how fast and in what direction velocity changes.
angular acceleration, α: The time derivative of angular velocity, α = dω/dt, measuring how quickly the rate of rotation changes.
angular frequency: The quantity ω in radians per second that sets the rate of oscillation in trigonometric motion functions.
angular position, θ: The radian angle specifying an object's rotational location, measured conventionally from the positive x-axis.
angular velocity: The rate of rotation of a frame or body, measured in rad/s and related to period by ω = 2π/T.
angular velocity, ω: The time derivative of angular position, ω = dθ/dt, giving the rate of rotation in radians per second.
antiderivative: A function whose derivative equals a given function, written ∫f(t) dt and unique only up to an added constant.
arc length: The total path distance traveled by a particle, found by integrating its instantaneous speed over time.
asymptotic approach: Behavior where a function gets arbitrarily close to a limiting value without ever reaching it in finite time.
atwood machine: Two masses joined by an inextensible rope over a single fixed pulley, used to study reduced effective gravitational acceleration.
boundary condition: A constraint on a function's value at a specific point, used to fix integration constants and select a unique solution.
centrifugal force: A fictitious force felt in a rotating frame, directed radially outward with magnitude mω²r, balancing the real centripetal force.
centripetal acceleration: The acceleration component pointing toward a circular path's center, magnitude a_c = v²/r = ω²r, continually changing velocity's direction.
centripetal force: The real net force an inertial observer identifies as pointing toward the circle's center, producing centripetal acceleration.
chain rule: The differentiation rule d/dt[f(g(t))] = f′(g(t))·g′(t), essential for differentiating trigonometric motion functions.
chain rule identity: The relation a = v·dv/dx, derived from a = (dv/dx)(dx/dt), useful when force depends on position.
chain rule identity for acceleration: The calculus relation a = v·dv/dx, applied when the force is a function of position rather than time.
characteristic time: The quantity m/b setting the timescale over which velocity changes significantly, the time for velocity to fall by a factor e.
closed orbit: A phase-space trajectory forming a closed loop, representing periodic motion that repeatedly returns to the same state.
complementary angles: Two launch angles θ and 90° − θ that give the same range on flat ground, since sin2θ = sin2(90° − θ).
component independence: The principle that perpendicular components of acceleration, velocity, and position evolve by separate equations linked only by shared time.
compound pulley system: A configuration with both fixed and movable pulleys, requiring constraint derivation from rope-length conservation to relate accelerations.
constant acceleration assumption: The built-in requirement that acceleration not vary with time, violated whenever force depends on velocity or position.
constant of integration: The undetermined constant arising in an indefinite integral, fixed by initial conditions to obtain a unique physical solution.
constraint equation: A mathematical relation from geometry that reduces independent variables, obtained in pulley problems by differentiating fixed rope length.
coriolis force: A fictitious force in a rotating frame perpendicular to an object's velocity, magnitude 2mωv, deflecting moving bodies sideways.
coupled differential equations: A system where variables appear across equations, so none can be solved alone and all must be solved simultaneously.
coupling node: A mass joining two or more independent rope subsystems, requiring multiple tensions and linking their separate constraints.
cross product: A vector operation yielding a vector perpendicular to both inputs, with magnitude equal to the product of magnitudes times sine of the angle.
cross-dependence: The presence of one direction's variable inside another direction's force expression, mathematically coupling the equations.
curvature: The reciprocal of the radius of curvature, measuring how sharply a path bends at each point.
diagnostic expansion: Writing out force components explicitly and identifying every variable in each to test whether the equations separate.
discretization: Converting a continuous function into a sequence of discrete values at set intervals, enabling numerical computation.
displacement: The change in position over a time interval, equal to the integral of velocity and able to be positive or negative.
distance traveled: The total path length covered, equal to the integral of speed (∫|v| dt) and always a nonnegative scalar.
equilibrium position: A location where net force and acceleration are zero, serving as the reference point for oscillatory motion.
equivalence principle: The principle that gravity and acceleration are locally indistinguishable, so no local experiment can separate them.
euler's method: A first-order numerical technique that updates variables by multiplying their derivatives by a small time step Δt.
exponential decay: A pattern of decrease by the same fraction each equal time interval, characterized by a negative-exponent function of e.
external force: A force exerted on a system by an agent outside it, such as gravity or a surface normal force, appearing in net-force calculations.
fictitious force: An apparent force introduced in a non-inertial frame, equal to −mA, arising from the frame's acceleration rather than a real interaction.
galilean transformation: Equations relating position and velocity between frames moving at constant relative velocity, r′ = r − v₀t and v′ = v − v₀.
graphical impulse calculation: Finding impulse as the area under a force-versus-time curve when analytic integration is impractical.
impulse: The time integral of force (∫F dt), equal to the change in momentum and measured in N·s or kg·m/s.
impulse-momentum theorem: The statement that the impulse delivered to an object equals its change in momentum, ∫F dt = mΔv.
indefinite integral: The antiderivative of a function plus an arbitrary constant, representing all functions whose derivative is the integrand.
independent constraint: A kinematic relation from one rope's fixed length, separate from other ropes' constraints and requiring its own differentiation.
inertial reference frame: A frame where Newton's laws hold without modification, characterized by zero acceleration relative to the distant stars.
inextensible rope: An idealized rope of fixed total length regardless of applied force, enabling constraint derivation through length conservation.
initial condition: A known value of position or velocity at a specific time, usually t = 0, used to determine integration constants.
initial conditions: Known position and velocity values at t = 0, used to fix integration constants when solving kinematic differential equations.
initial slope: The tangent of the launch angle θ, equal to dy/dx evaluated at x = 0, setting the trajectory's initial direction.
initial value problem: A differential equation paired with initial conditions that together determine a unique solution, the standard kinematics form.
instantaneous acceleration: The derivative of velocity with respect to time, a = dv/dt, or equivalently the second derivative of position, at a single instant.
instantaneous velocity: The derivative of position with respect to time, v = dx/dt, giving the exact velocity at a single instant rather than an average.
integrand: The function inside the integral sign that is being summed over with respect to the variable of integration.
integration constant: The arbitrary constant C produced by indefinite integration, which must be fixed by initial conditions to get a unique solution.
integration limits: The starting and ending values of the variable over which a definite integral is evaluated, the interval of interest.
internal force: A force one part of a system exerts on another part, such as rope tension, which cancels when summing forces over the whole system.
kinematic equations: Algebraic relations v = v₀ + at and x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² derived by integrating constant acceleration, valid only when acceleration is constant.
lift force: A force perpendicular to velocity that makes a force in one direction depend on perpendicular velocity, coupling the x and y equations.
linear drag: A resistive force proportional to velocity, of the form F = −bv, where b is the drag coefficient in kg/s.
lorentz force: The force F = q(E + v × B) on a charged particle in electromagnetic fields, whose magnetic term couples motion through a cross product.
magnitude: The length of a vector, always nonnegative, computed from perpendicular components using the Pythagorean theorem.
mechanical advantage: The ratio of output force to input force of a machine, traded against displacement so that force times displacement stays constant.
movable pulley: A pulley free to translate rather than fixed to a support, producing acceleration ratios that are not one-to-one.
non-inertial reference frame: A frame accelerating relative to an inertial one, requiring fictitious forces to apply Newton's second law correctly.
non-uniform circular motion: Circular motion with changing speed, characterized by α ≠ 0 and needing both centripetal and tangential acceleration components.
optimization: A calculus technique finding maxima or minima by setting the first derivative to zero and classifying critical points with the second derivative.
parabolic trajectory: The quadratic path of a projectile under constant gravity with no air resistance, a downward-opening parabola.
parameter elimination: An algebraic technique that solves one parametric equation for the parameter and substitutes to relate the dependent variables directly.
parametric equations: A pair of functions x(t) and y(t) that specify each coordinate separately as a function of time.
parametric equations of motion: Position functions x(t) and y(t) found by integrating acceleration components twice with appropriate initial conditions.
path integral: An integral evaluated along a curve, with an integrand that depends on position along the path.
phase relationship: A fixed angular offset between oscillating quantities; in simple harmonic motion velocity leads position by 90 degrees.
phase space: A mathematical space whose coordinates are position and velocity, where each point represents a complete dynamical state.
phase trajectory: The path a system traces in phase space as it evolves, encoding its full position–velocity history without explicit time.
position variable: A coordinate assigned to each moving mass in a coupled system, measured from a fixed point to express rope lengths algebraically.
position vector: The vector r(t) from the origin to an object's location, written in circular motion as r cosθ î + r sinθ ĵ.
position-dependent force: A force whose magnitude or direction varies with where the object is, such as a spring force or gravitational field.
power rule: The differentiation rule that the derivative of tⁿ is n·tⁿ⁻¹, applied term by term to polynomial functions.
pseudoforce: Another name for a fictitious force, emphasizing that no physical object pushes or pulls to create it.
radial unit vector: A unit vector pointing outward from the circle's center to the object, equal to cosθ î + sinθ ĵ.
radian: The SI angle unit defined so that an arc length equal to the radius subtends one radian, making s = rθ an identity.
radians per second: The SI unit of angular velocity, required so that v = rω and a = rα yield correct SI linear quantities.
radius of curvature: The radius of the circle that best locally approximates a path at a given point, setting how sharply it bends.
range: The horizontal distance R a projectile travels back to its original height, given by R = v₀²sin2θ/g under constant acceleration.
reference frame: A coordinate system attached to an observer, providing the origin and axes for measuring position, velocity, and acceleration.
restoring acceleration: Acceleration directed toward the equilibrium position, proportional to and opposite the displacement, characteristic of simple harmonic motion.
revolutions per minute, rpm: A common engineering unit of angular velocity, converted to rad/s by multiplying by 2π/60.
right-hand rule: A convention for finding a cross product's direction by curling the right hand's fingers from the first vector to the second.
scalar quantity: A physical quantity fully specified by a numerical value with no directional information.
second-order differential equation: An equation containing the second time derivative of position, arising when force depends on position and velocity.
separable equations: A system in which each equation contains only its own variable, allowing each to be solved independently.
separation of variables: A technique for solving a differential equation by grouping each variable on one side and integrating both sides independently.
simultaneous equations: A set of algebraic equations with multiple unknowns that must be solved together, as in coupled Newton's-law and constraint systems.
speed: The scalar magnitude of the velocity vector, computed as the square root of the sum of squared velocity components.
supporting rope segments: The number of separate rope sections bearing a movable pulley's load, directly setting the acceleration ratio.
system approach: A method treating connected bodies as one composite system so internal forces cancel, reducing the problem to net external force over total mass.
tangential acceleration: The acceleration component directed along the circular path, magnitude a_t = rα, responsible for changing the object's speed.
tangential unit vector: A unit vector pointing along the direction of motion on a circle, perpendicular to the radial vector, equal to −sinθ î + cosθ ĵ.
tension variable: An unknown force magnitude assigned to each independent rope segment, found by solving Newton's-law and constraint equations together.
terminal velocity: The constant velocity reached when drag exactly balances the driving force, where dv/dt = 0.
time step: The interval Δt between successive calculations in numerical integration; smaller values give greater accuracy but more steps.
time-dependent force: A force whose magnitude or direction changes as time passes according to a specified function F(t).
trajectory equation: The function y(x) obtained by eliminating time from parametric equations, revealing the geometric path shape.
truncation error: The systematic error in Euler's method from assuming the derivative stays constant over each step, accumulating across many steps.
turning point: A position where velocity is zero and the particle reverses direction, appearing as a crossing of the position axis in phase space.
uniform circular motion: Circular motion at constant speed, where α = 0 and a_t = 0, leaving only centripetal acceleration.
validity conditions: The physical assumptions, such as constant acceleration and flat ground, under which a derived formula correctly describes a system.
variable acceleration: Acceleration that changes with time, position, or velocity, requiring integration of a(t) rather than constant-acceleration formulas.
vector differential equation: An equation relating derivatives of vector quantities, which expands into several scalar equations in component form.
vector quantity: A physical quantity requiring both magnitude and direction for complete specification.
velocity vector: The time derivative of position, v(t) = dr/dt, giving both the speed and direction of motion at each instant.
work-energy relationship: The connection between force integrated over displacement and the change in kinetic energy, arising from the chain-rule form of Newton's second law.
accumulated change: The total change of a quantity obtained by integrating its rate of change over a time interval, contrasted with an instantaneous rate.
accumulation: The mathematical process by which infinitesimal contributions sum through integration into a finite total, as dp = F·dt builds total momentum change.
adaptive step size: An advanced technique that automatically adjusts Δt during a simulation based on local error estimates, improving efficiency while keeping accuracy.
amplitude: The constant A in x(t) = A·cos(ωt + φ), giving the maximum displacement from equilibrium in meters.
apparent weight: The normal force a support exerts on an object, which differs from true gravitational weight when the system accelerates.
asymptotic behavior: The tendency of a function to approach a limiting value as its argument grows without bound, as velocity nears v_T.
average force approximation: An incorrect method that averages endpoint force values and multiplies by time, failing for nonlinear force functions since the endpoint average is not the integral.
banking angle: The angle by which a roadway surface is tilted from horizontal, measured so the surface slopes downward toward the turn's center.
closed-form solution: An explicit expression for position or velocity in terms of standard functions, obtainable by directly integrating the differential equation.
coefficient of kinetic friction: The dimensionless ratio μ_k = f_k/N characterizing sliding friction, nearly constant and independent of sliding speed for a surface pair.
coefficient of static friction: The dimensionless ratio μ_s = f_{s,max}/N characterizing maximum static friction, always larger than μ_k for the same surfaces.
constraint force: A force that adjusts its magnitude to satisfy a physical constraint; static friction, normal force, and tension are constraint forces.
constraint relationship: An equation linking the motion of different parts of a system, such as equal acceleration magnitudes for masses on an inextensible rope.
coordinate convention: The choice of which direction is positive in a problem, fixing the sign of every force term and requiring consistent application.
coupled equations: Equations in which unknowns appear together, requiring substitution or matrix methods, as when normal force links horizontal and vertical balance.
critical point: A position in circular motion where the normal force reaches an extreme, typically zero at the threshold of losing surface contact.
definite integral: An integral evaluated between specific limits, yielding a numerical accumulation over a given interval, such as ∫ from t₁ to t₂ of F(t) dt.
deflection: The bending of an object's path by a force perpendicular to its velocity, such as Coriolis deflection (right in the Northern Hemisphere).
differential form of newton's second law: The equation F = m·dv/dt expressing acceleration as the instantaneous rate of change of velocity, enabling integration when force varies.
double atwood machine: A compound pulley system where one pulley supports another, creating coupled constraints relative to a moving reference.
drag coefficient c_d: A dimensionless number characterizing a shape's drag efficiency, appearing in the quadratic drag coefficient c = ½·C_d·ρ·A.
drag force: The resistive force a fluid exerts on a moving object, opposite the velocity, arising from viscous friction and pressure differences.
dummy variable of integration: A temporary variable used inside a definite integral that does not appear in the final answer, often written t′ when the upper limit is t.
effective gravity: The vector sum of true gravitational and centrifugal acceleration at Earth's surface, varying with latitude and smallest at the equator.
elastic potential energy: The energy stored in a deformed spring, equal to ½kx², derived by integrating the spring force over displacement.
elementary functions: The standard set of polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions and their inverses forming closed-form expressions.
equilibrium condition: The requirement that net force be zero on a non-accelerating object, with horizontal and vertical net forces each independently zero in two dimensions.
equilibrium stretch: The distance δ a vertical spring stretches to support a resting mass, set by kδ = mg.
euler method: A first-order numerical integration technique that steps along the tangent line, using current position and velocity to estimate the next step's values.
exponential approach: The behavior v(t) = v_T(1 − e^(−t/τ)) describing velocity nearing terminal velocity asymptotically but never reaching it in finite time.
first order accuracy: A classification indicating global error proportional to the first power of step size, characteristic of the basic Euler method.
first-order linear ode: A differential equation containing only the first derivative of the unknown function appearing to the first power, guaranteeing an analytic solution.
force balance equation: Newton's second law written as m(dv/dt) = sum of forces, serving as the starting point for deriving equations of motion.
force components: The projections of a force vector onto coordinate axes; for force F at angle θ above horizontal, F·cosθ horizontally and F·sinθ vertically.
forward euler scheme: The standard implementation that updates velocity with current acceleration before updating position, distinct from the symplectic variant.
foucault pendulum: A long pendulum demonstrating Earth's rotation through the apparent precession of its swing plane, at rate ω·sinφ for latitude φ.
general solution: The complete family of functions satisfying a differential equation, containing arbitrary constants later fixed by initial conditions.
geometric constraint: A kinematic relation imposed by the physical arrangement of ropes, pulleys, or surfaces, limiting how parts of a system can move.
global accumulated error: The total deviation between numerical approximation and exact solution after all steps, proportional to the first power of Δt in Euler's method.
hooke's law: The linear relation F = −kx between spring force and displacement, where k is the spring constant and the minus sign opposes displacement.
hyperbolic tangent function: The function tanh(x) = (eˣ − e^(−x))/(eˣ + e^(−x)), describing approach to terminal velocity under quadratic drag.
ideal banking equation: The relation tanθ = v²/(rg) linking banking angle θ to ideal speed v, turn radius r, and gravitational acceleration g.
ideal pulley: A massless, frictionless pulley that changes a rope's direction without changing tension magnitude, unlike real pulleys with mass and friction.
ideal speed: The speed at which a vehicle can round a banked curve with zero friction, where the normal force's horizontal component supplies the needed centripetal force.
impending slip direction: The direction a vehicle would begin to slide if friction were insufficient; friction always acts opposite this impending slip.
kinetic friction: The friction force on an object sliding across a surface, with fixed magnitude f_k = μ_k·N, where μ_k is the kinetic friction coefficient.
latitude: The north–south angular position from the equator, from 0° at the equator to 90° at the poles, on which Coriolis and centrifugal effects depend.
linear drag model: A fluid-resistance model where drag is directly proportional to velocity (F_d = bv), valid for slow objects at low Reynolds number.
linear mass density: The mass per unit length of an extended object such as a rope, denoted λ with SI units kg/m.
local application of newton's second law: Applying F = ma to an arbitrary segment rather than the whole continuum, revealing how internal forces vary with position.
local truncation error: The deviation a single numerical step introduces compared to the exact solution, proportional to Δt² in Euler's method.
massive rope: A rope with non-negligible mass that must be accelerated, causing tension to vary along its length rather than stay constant.
maximum speed on banked curve: The highest speed a vehicle can round a banked curve without sliding outward, where static friction is maximal and points down-slope toward center.
maximum velocity: The speed of an oscillator passing through equilibrium, equal to Aω, occurring when all energy is kinetic and potential energy is zero.
minimum speed condition: The speed at a circular motion's critical point where normal force or tension becomes zero, equal to √(rg) at the top of a vertical loop.
minimum speed on banked curve: The lowest speed a vehicle can round a banked curve without sliding inward, where static friction is maximal and points up-slope away from center.
natural length: The unstretched length of a spring with no force applied, the reference for measuring total spring deformation in a vertical system.
net force: The vector sum of all forces acting on an object, equal to mass times acceleration by Newton's second law.
non-uniform mass distribution: A mass distribution whose linear density varies with position, requiring integration rather than simple multiplication to find segment mass.
nonlinear differential equation: A differential equation where the unknown or its derivatives appear to powers other than one or multiply each other, blocking superposition.
normal force: The contact force perpendicular to a surface that prevents objects from passing through each other, a constraint force adjusting to other forces.
normal force in vertical loops: The surface contact force on an object, always pointing toward the loop's center—upward at the bottom and downward at the top.
optimal angle: The angle θ = arctan(μ_k) minimizing the force to slide an object, perfectly balancing reduced normal force against horizontal propulsion.
period: The time T = 2π/ω for one complete oscillation cycle, independent of amplitude in simple harmonic motion.
phase constant: The constant φ in radians within the solution, setting the oscillator's position at t = 0 and determined by initial conditions.
phase shift: The displacement of a sinusoidal function along the time axis, controlled by phase constant φ and setting when maximum displacement occurs.
plumb bob: A weight hung on a string that aligns with effective gravity; because effective gravity includes centrifugal contribution, it does not point to Earth's center except at the poles.
power rule for integration: The rule ∫ tⁿ dt = t^(n+1)/(n+1) + C, used to integrate polynomial force functions term by term.
precession: The gradual rotation of a plane or axis, as in a Foucault pendulum's swing plane, with precession rate ω·sinφ.
quadratic drag model: A fluid-resistance model where drag is proportional to velocity squared (F_d = cv²), valid for fast objects at high Reynolds number.
radial direction: The direction toward or away from the rotation axis; centripetal acceleration points radially inward, centrifugal force radially outward.
recalculation: The essential numerical step of recomputing acceleration from current position and velocity before advancing to the next time step.
relative acceleration: An object's acceleration measured in a frame attached to another accelerating body, added to that frame's acceleration to get absolute acceleration.
release from rest: The initial condition v₀ = 0, for which using the cosine form gives φ = 0 and A equal to the initial displacement.
restoring force: Any force acting to return a system to equilibrium, always directed opposite the displacement from the equilibrium position.
reynolds number: A dimensionless quantity giving the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in fluid flow, determining whether linear or quadratic drag dominates.
runge-kutta methods: A family of higher-order numerical integration techniques evaluating the derivative at several points per step for greater accuracy than Euler's.
second derivative test: A method classifying a critical point: a negative second derivative there indicates a maximum, a positive one indicates a minimum.
segment isolation: A technique drawing an imaginary boundary in a continuum to analyze forces on one part as if it were a separate system.
separable differential equation: A first-order ODE rewritable with all terms of one variable on one side and the other variable on the opposite side, integrated independently.
shifted equilibrium: The new rest position of a spring–mass system under a constant external force like gravity, about which oscillation occurs at unchanged angular frequency.
simple harmonic oscillator equation: The second-order differential equation d²x/dt² = −ω²·x describing any system whose restoring force is proportional to displacement.
state variables: Quantities such as position and velocity that fully characterize a mechanical system's instantaneous state and may appear in force expressions.
static friction: The friction force on an object at rest relative to a surface, ranging from zero up to μ_s·N to maintain equilibrium.
static friction on inclines: Friction preventing relative motion between surfaces; on banked curves it has both horizontal and vertical components in both Newton's-law equations.
stokes' law: The relation b = 6πηr giving the drag coefficient for a sphere of radius r moving slowly through a fluid of viscosity η.
system boundary: An imaginary closed surface drawn around one or more bodies, determining which interactions count as external forces and which are internal.
system of equations: Several equations that must be satisfied simultaneously; connected systems typically need as many equations as unknowns, solved by substitution or matrices.
tangent line approximation: The geometric interpretation of an Euler step, where motion follows a straight segment parallel to the instantaneous velocity vector rather than the true curve.
taylor series expansion: Representation of a smooth function as an infinite sum of terms using its successive derivatives at a point, used to analyze truncation error.
tension: The pulling force transmitted through a rope or cable; in an ideal massless rope tension is uniform throughout, acting as a constraint force.
threshold condition: A limiting case where a constraint variable such as normal force, friction, or tension reaches zero or its maximum, often simplifying analysis.
time step delta t: The discrete interval between successive calculations in a numerical method, chosen small enough for accuracy yet large enough for efficiency.
total mechanical energy: The sum of kinetic and potential energy, conserved at ½kA² throughout simple harmonic motion when no dissipative forces act.
trial solution: A proposed mathematical form for a differential equation's solution, then substituted into the original equation to verify it.
update equations: The explicit formulas expressing new position and velocity from current values and the time step, forming the computational core of Euler's method.
verlet integration: A numerical method especially suited to conservative systems, conserving energy better than standard Euler over long simulations.
weightlessness in circular motion: The sensation experienced when normal force is zero, as at the top of a loop at minimum speed where the surface exerts no force.
zero crossing: The instant a force function changes sign through zero, corresponding to zero acceleration but generally not zero velocity.
allowed region: The set of positions where potential energy U(x) is at or below total energy E, marking where a particle can physically go.
apoapsis: The point in an orbit farthest from the central mass, whose distance r_a contributes to computing the semi-major axis.
average efficiency: The total useful work output divided by total energy input over an interval, found by integrating both power functions and taking the ratio.
average power: Total work divided by elapsed time, P_avg = W_total/Δt, requiring integration of the instantaneous power function over the interval.
beat frequency: The frequency at which energy oscillates between two coupled oscillators, equal to the absolute difference of the two normal-mode frequencies.
beat period: The time for one complete cycle of energy exchange between coupled oscillators, the reciprocal of the beat frequency.
binomial approximation: The approximation (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx for small x, used to linearize expressions such as gravitational field variations near Earth.
bound motion: Motion confined to a finite region because total energy is below the potential needed to escape, such as a closed orbit.
bound state: A state with negative total mechanical energy, in which an object cannot escape to infinity and remains gravitationally trapped.
center-to-center distance: The separation between the centers of two masses, the relevant distance r in Newton's law of universal gravitation.
closed loop work: The total work done by a force around a closed path, which is zero for any conservative force.
closed-loop integral: A line integral evaluated around a closed path, equal to zero for a conservative force field.
component work: The work contributed by a single force component, the product of that component and displacement along its direction.
conservative force: A force whose work depends only on endpoints, not path, and around any closed loop is zero, allowing a potential energy to be defined.
constant power system: A system delivering fixed power, so force decreases as speed increases, since power equals force times velocity.
coupled motion: Motion in which the dynamics of one part influence another through forces or constraints, requiring simultaneous analysis.
coupled oscillators: Two or more oscillators linked so that energy transfers between them, producing normal modes and beats.
coupling constant: A parameter quantifying the strength of interaction between coupled oscillators, setting the rate of energy exchange.
curl condition: The requirement that a force field's curl vanish, the test for whether the force is conservative.
displacement vector: The vector from an object's initial to final position, whose dot product with force gives work.
dissipated power: The rate at which mechanical energy is converted to heat by non-conservative forces such as friction or drag.
dissipation: The irreversible loss of mechanical energy to heat or other forms through non-conservative forces.
dot product: A scalar operation equal to the product of two vectors' magnitudes times the cosine of the angle between them, defining work.
driven oscillator: An oscillator subjected to an external periodic force, whose response depends on how the driving frequency compares to its natural frequency.
eccentricity independence: The fact that an orbit's total energy depends only on the semi-major axis, not on its eccentricity.
effective spring constant k_eff: The single equivalent stiffness representing a combination of springs, found by combining series or parallel spring constants.
energy dissipation: The conversion of mechanical energy into non-recoverable forms such as heat by non-conservative forces.
energy equation: An equation expressing conservation of mechanical energy, equating total energy at one state to that at another.
energy input: The total energy supplied to a system, against which useful output is compared to determine efficiency.
energy method: A problem-solving approach using conservation of energy rather than forces to relate states of a system.
energy transfer period: The time over which energy fully shifts from one coupled oscillator to another and back.
equations of motion: The differential equations, derived from Newton's second law, governing how a system's position evolves in time.
escape energy: The minimum total energy, exactly zero, an object needs to just escape a gravitational field to infinity.
escape velocity: The minimum speed an object needs to escape a body's gravity without further propulsion, √(2GM/r) and independent of the object's mass.
field strength variation: The change in gravitational field strength with distance, decreasing as the inverse square of separation from the source.
forbidden region: The set of positions where potential energy exceeds total energy, which a particle cannot enter.
frequency response curve: A plot of an oscillator's amplitude versus driving frequency, peaking sharply at resonance.
frequency splitting: The separation of a coupled system's single natural frequency into two distinct normal-mode frequencies.
gradient: A vector operator giving the direction and rate of steepest increase of a scalar function, such as potential energy.
gradient of potential energy: The negative gradient of potential energy, equal to the conservative force, F = −∇U.
gravitational binding: The condition of negative total energy that keeps an object gravitationally bound to a central mass.
gravitationally bound: Describing a system with negative total energy, unable to separate to infinity.
in phase mode: A normal mode of coupled oscillators in which both masses move together in the same direction.
infinitesimal work: The tiny amount of work dW = F·dr done over an infinitesimal displacement, integrated to give total work.
instantaneous efficiency: The ratio of useful power output to power input at a single instant.
instantaneous power: The rate of doing work at a given instant, P = F·v, the time derivative of work.
integration constant c: The arbitrary constant C arising from indefinite integration, fixed by a known condition such as a reference point.
integration for potential energy: Computing potential energy by integrating the negative of a conservative force over displacement.
integration of products: Integrating a product of functions, often handled by integration by parts or substitution.
kinematic constraint: A relation restricting the motion of system parts, such as rolling without slipping or fixed rope length.
launch phase: The portion of motion during which propulsion acts, before an object coasts under gravity alone.
line integral: An integral of a function along a curve, used to compute work as force integrated along the path.
linearization error: The error introduced by approximating a nonlinear function with its tangent line near a point.
marginally unbound: The borderline case of exactly zero total energy, where an object just barely escapes with zero speed at infinity.
mass independence of escape velocity: The fact that escape velocity depends only on the central body's mass and radius, not on the escaping object's mass.
maximum kinetic energy: The greatest kinetic energy in a motion, occurring where potential energy is lowest, such as at equilibrium.
mechanical energy: The sum of kinetic and potential energy of a system, conserved when only conservative forces act.
near-earth approximation: Treating gravitational acceleration as constant g near Earth's surface, valid when height is small compared to Earth's radius.
negative power: Power delivered when force opposes velocity, removing energy from an object, as friction does.
neutral equilibrium: An equilibrium where potential energy is locally flat, so a displaced object neither returns nor moves further.
non-conservative force: A force whose work depends on the path taken, such as friction, dissipating mechanical energy.
normal mode: A pattern of oscillation in which all parts of a coupled system move sinusoidally at a single shared frequency.
normal mode coordinates: Combinations of displacements that decouple coupled oscillator equations into independent simple harmonic oscillators.
orbital energy formula: The relation E = −GMm/(2a) giving the total energy of an orbit in terms of the semi-major axis a.
oscillation amplitude: The maximum displacement from equilibrium during an oscillation.
out of phase mode: A normal mode in which the two coupled masses move in opposite directions.
partial derivative: The derivative of a multivariable function with respect to one variable while holding the others fixed.
path dependence: The property of a non-conservative force that the work done depends on the route taken between endpoints.
path dependent work: Work whose value changes with the chosen path, characteristic of non-conservative forces.
path independence: The property of a conservative force that work depends only on endpoints, not the route taken.
periapsis: The point in an orbit closest to the central mass, whose distance contributes to the semi-major axis.
phase response: How the phase of a driven oscillator's motion lags the driving force, varying with the driving frequency.
piecewise function: A function defined by different expressions over different intervals of its domain.
position-dependent acceleration: Acceleration that varies with position, requiring the chain-rule identity a = v·dv/dx to solve.
positive power: Power delivered when force acts along the velocity, adding energy to an object.
potential energy function: A function U(x) giving stored energy as a function of position, whose negative gradient is the conservative force.
potential well: A region where potential energy has a local minimum, trapping a particle in bound oscillatory motion.
power: The rate of doing work or transferring energy, P = dW/dt, measured in watts.
power function: A function of the form xⁿ, or a function describing how power varies with time or velocity.
power limited motion: Motion constrained by a maximum available power, so acceleration falls as speed rises.
power loss: The rate at which energy is dissipated from a system, reducing its useful power output.
quadratic scaling: A relationship in which one quantity varies with the square of another, such as kinetic energy with speed.
reference point: A chosen location where potential energy is defined to be zero, fixing the integration constant.
reference point at infinity: The convention of setting gravitational potential energy to zero at infinite separation, giving negative values for bound states.
regenerative efficiency: The fraction of energy recovered by a system that captures and reuses energy normally dissipated.
resonance: The large-amplitude response of a driven oscillator when the driving frequency matches its natural frequency.
semi-major axis: Half the longest diameter of an elliptical orbit, the average of periapsis and apoapsis distances, setting the orbital energy.
signed area: The area under a curve counted as positive above and negative below the axis, representing a definite integral.
slope interpretation: Reading the slope of a graph as a derivative, such as velocity from a position–time graph.
square root velocity dependence: A relationship in which a quantity, such as escape or critical speed, varies with the square root of another variable.
stable equilibrium: An equilibrium at a potential energy minimum, where a displaced object experiences a restoring force back toward it.
stopping distance: The distance an object travels while decelerating to rest, found from work–energy or kinematic analysis.
superposition: The principle that solutions of a linear system add, so combined motions are the sum of individual ones.
system kinetic energy: The total kinetic energy of all parts of a system, summing individual contributions.
total mechanical energy e: The conserved sum E of kinetic and potential energy, negative for gravitationally bound orbits.
unbound motion: Motion with total energy at or above zero, allowing an object to escape to infinity.
universal gravitational potential energy: The energy U = −GMm/r of two masses, taken zero at infinite separation and negative for bound configurations.
unstable equilibrium: An equilibrium at a potential energy maximum, where a displaced object is pushed further from it.
variable force: A force whose magnitude or direction changes with position, time, or velocity, requiring integration to find work.
work: The energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement, W = ∫F·dr, measured in joules.
work by friction: The negative work done by friction, equal to friction force times sliding distance, dissipating energy as heat.
work capacity: The maximum work a system can perform, set by its available stored energy.
work integral: The integral W = ∫F·dr giving total work done by a variable force along a path.
work-energy graph: A graph relating work or force to displacement, whose area represents work and energy change.
work-energy theorem: The statement that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
angular momentum of a particle: The quantity L = r × p, the cross product of position and linear momentum, measuring rotational motion about a point.
arc length element: An infinitesimal piece ds of a curved path, integrated to find total arc length.
center of mass frame: A reference frame moving with the system's center of mass, in which total momentum is zero.
center of mass reference: The center of mass used as the origin for analyzing a system's motion and rotation.
center of mass velocity: The velocity of a system's center of mass, equal to total momentum divided by total mass.
centroid: The geometric center of a shape, coinciding with the center of mass for uniform density.
closed system: A system exchanging no mass or net external force with its surroundings, so total momentum is conserved.
common final velocity: The single shared velocity of objects that stick together after a perfectly inelastic collision.
conservation of angular momentum: The principle that a system's total angular momentum stays constant when no net external torque acts.
conservation of kinetic energy: The condition, holding only in elastic collisions, that total kinetic energy is unchanged by the interaction.
conservation of momentum: The principle that total linear momentum of a system stays constant when no net external force acts.
contact point reference: Choosing the instantaneous point of contact as the axis for torque or angular momentum analysis, as in rolling.
continuous mass transfer: The ongoing flow of mass into or out of a system, as in a rocket ejecting exhaust.
difference of squares identity: The algebraic identity a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), used to simplify elastic-collision velocity expressions.
double integration: Integrating twice, as when finding position from acceleration or computing properties over a two-dimensional region.
elastic collision: A collision conserving both momentum and kinetic energy, in which objects rebound without energy loss.
elastic collision velocity formulas: The expressions giving each object's final velocity after a one-dimensional elastic collision from the masses and initial velocities.
energy dissipation in mass transfer: The kinetic energy lost when mass is transferred and accelerated, as in inelastic accretion.
exhaust velocity: The speed of ejected propellant relative to a rocket, determining the thrust it produces.
force from mass accretion: The force arising as a system gains mass, equal to the rate of mass gain times relative velocity.
frame transformation: Converting velocities or positions between reference frames moving relative to each other.
geometric slice: A thin strip or element of a body chosen to set up an integral for mass, center of mass, or moment of inertia.
horizontal strip element: A thin horizontal element of an area, used as dm or dA in integrations over a two-dimensional shape.
infinitesimal mass element dm: A tiny piece of a body's mass, summed by integration to compute total mass or moments.
internal redistribution: A rearrangement of mass or momentum within a system that leaves total momentum unchanged.
kinetic energy loss: The decrease in kinetic energy during an inelastic collision, converted to heat, sound, or deformation.
lab frame: The reference frame fixed to the laboratory or ground in which measurements are made.
limiting case analysis: Checking a result by examining extreme values of parameters to verify physical reasonableness.
linear mass density lambda: The mass per unit length λ of a one-dimensional object, used as dm = λ dx in integrals.
mass flow rate: The rate dm/dt at which mass enters or leaves a system, central to variable-mass dynamics.
mass ratio: The ratio of a rocket's initial to final mass, appearing in the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation.
mass weighted position: Position weighted by mass, summed and divided by total mass to locate the center of mass.
newton's second law for rotation: The rotational analog τ = Iα, stating net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.
orbital angular momentum: The angular momentum of a body due to its motion about an external axis, as opposed to spin.
parallel axis theorem: The relation I = I_cm + Md² giving the moment of inertia about any axis from the center-of-mass value.
perfectly inelastic collision: A collision in which objects stick together, conserving momentum but losing the maximum possible kinetic energy.
perpendicular distance: The shortest distance from an axis to a line of action of force or momentum, the lever arm in torque and angular momentum.
pivot torque analysis: Analyzing torques about a chosen pivot point to determine rotational equilibrium or motion.
position dependent density: A density that varies with position, requiring integration to compute mass and center of mass.
rebound: The bouncing back of an object after a collision, occurring with reversed or reduced velocity.
relative velocity of approach: The rate at which two objects close in before a collision, equal in magnitude to the separation velocity in an elastic collision.
relative velocity of separation: The rate at which two objects move apart after a collision, equal to the approach velocity for an elastic collision.
right hand rule for cross products: A convention for finding a cross product's direction by pointing the right hand's fingers from the first vector toward the second.
ring element: A thin annular element of a disk or sphere used as dm in integrals for mass or moment of inertia.
rolling without slipping: Motion where the contact point is instantaneously at rest, linking translation and rotation by v = rω.
second-order infinitesimal: A product of two infinitesimals, negligible compared to first-order terms and dropped in derivations.
spin angular momentum: The angular momentum of a body due to rotation about its own center of mass.
surface mass density sigma: The mass per unit area σ of a two-dimensional object, used as dm = σ dA in integrals.
thrust: The forward force on a rocket from ejecting propellant, equal to exhaust velocity times mass flow rate.
total angular momentum: The sum of spin and orbital angular momentum of a system about a chosen axis.
tsiolkovsky rocket equation: The relation Δv = v_e·ln(m_i/m_f) giving a rocket's velocity change from exhaust speed and mass ratio.
two term decomposition: Splitting a quantity into two contributions, such as translational and rotational kinetic energy, for separate analysis.
underdetermined system: A system with fewer equations than unknowns, requiring an additional condition such as energy conservation to solve.
uniform distribution: A distribution of constant density, so mass is proportional to length, area, or volume.
variable density distribution: A mass distribution whose density varies with position, requiring integration to find total mass and center of mass.
variable-mass system: A system whose mass changes over time, such as a rocket, analyzed with the thrust equation F = m dv/dt − v_rel dm/dt.
velocity exchange: The result of a one-dimensional elastic collision between equal masses, in which the two objects swap velocities.
velocity reversal: A change of an object's velocity to the opposite direction, as in an elastic bounce off a fixed wall.
